sections.heading: Coming to you with nothing to hide
sections.text: Everlasting Father and Creator, I come to you as I really am. Left to myself, I have ruined myself. Sin has reached deeper than my actions; it has twisted my desires, weakened my will, clouded my mind, and made me far less than what you made me to be. I do not come with strength to offer you or goodness to bargain with. My only hope is you.
theological_themes: Human sin is not merely external wrongdoing but inward corruption and helplessness before God.
Hope rests not in self-improvement or moral strength, but in God himself.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the inability of the sinful self to produce true righteousness before God. This supports the prayer’s honest confession that sin has affected the whole person and that self-rescue is impossible.
David’s prayer recognizes deep inward sin and asks God for a clean heart. It grounds the movement from confession of defilement to dependence on God’s renewing mercy.

sections.heading: Depending on mercy I could never deserve
sections.text: If I am saved, it will not be because I deserved it or managed to make myself acceptable. It will be because your mercy is far greater than my sin, and your grace is richer than I can measure. You have not shown yourself to be reluctant or cold toward sinners who turn to you. You have revealed a heart of peace toward your people and have made a way to rescue me from the destruction my sin deserves, and to bring me back into joy, safety, and dignity before you.
theological_themes: Salvation is entirely by undeserved grace and abundant mercy.
God’s saving purpose is not evil toward his people, but peace and restoration through his own provision.

scripture_references.connection: This passage emphasizes God’s rich mercy and grace as the source of salvation, explicitly excluding human boasting. It directly supports the prayer’s dependence on undeserved mercy rather than personal merit.

In context, God speaks to his exiled covenant people with purposes of future restoration rather than abandonment. While not a blanket promise of ease, it fits the prayer’s trust that God’s saving intentions are ultimately peace, not destruction.

sections.heading: Thanking you for the Mediator you appointed
sections.text: Father, thank you for your eternal saving purpose and for giving me a Mediator, Jesus Christ. Thank you that he did not turn back, grow weary, or fail in the work you gave him. He carried it all the way to the cross, and there he could truly say, “It is finished.” Because of him, your justice has not been ignored, your truth has not been compromised, and your holy law has not been treated as small. In Christ, you have laid a solid foundation for my hope.
theological_themes: God appointed Christ as the one Mediator between God and sinners.
Christ completed the saving work given to him, satisfying divine justice and establishing a secure ground of hope.

scripture_references.connection: Paul identifies Jesus as the one Mediator who gave himself as a ransom. This directly grounds the prayer’s gratitude that God appointed a Mediator for sinners.
Jesus’ cry from the cross declares the completion of his redemptive work. It supports the prayer’s confidence that the work given to Christ was fully accomplished.
Paul explains that God justifies sinners through Christ’s redemption while demonstrating his righteousness. This illuminates the prayer’s claim that God’s justice is satisfied rather than bypassed.

sections.heading: Receiving Christ’s work as mine
sections.text: Lord Jesus, I look to you not only as a Savior in general, but as my Savior. You have taken what was mine—my grief, guilt, sorrow, and brokenness—and you have given what I could never win for myself: peace with God and healing for my soul. Because of your blood, I am justified. Because you live, I am kept and saved. I glory in your cross, and I gladly bow under your rule. By your Spirit, teach me to think, love, and desire as you do.
theological_themes: Faith personally receives Christ and his saving benefits.
Christ’s death brings justification and peace; his risen life secures ongoing salvation.
Those saved by Christ’s cross also submit to his lordship and are formed by his Spirit.

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah speaks of the Servant bearing griefs, carrying sorrows, and bringing peace and healing through his suffering. The prayer draws directly on this substitutionary language as fulfilled in Christ.

Paul connects justification by faith, peace with God, justification by Christ’s blood, and salvation through his life. This strongly supports the prayer’s movement from the cross to present assurance in the living Christ.
Paul teaches that believers receive the Spirit and, in that sense, have the mind of Christ. This grounds the prayer’s request to be inwardly shaped by Christ through the Spirit.

sections.heading: Asking for a whole-life faith that lasts
sections.text: Lord, do not let my faith be something I pick up only at certain moments or only in certain parts of life. Let it reach every corner of me—my thoughts, habits, words, relationships, work, choices, and hidden motives. Make it real, active, and fruitful. Keep me close to your Word and faithful in the work you give me to do, so that I may finish my race in peace and come safely to the end you have prepared for me.
theological_themes: True faith is not occasional or compartmentalized but shapes the whole life.
Perseverance involves abiding in Christ’s word and walking in the good works God gives.
The believer asks God for grace to finish faithfully and die in peace.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says true disciples abide in his word. This supports the prayer’s desire not merely to admire God’s truth, but to continue in it as the mark of genuine discipleship.
Paul calls believers to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. This grounds the prayer’s request for faith to affect every part of life, not only explicitly religious moments.
Paul looks back on a completed race and a kept faith. This fits the prayer’s longing to reach the end faithfully and in peace.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s reference to the “everlasting covenant” reflects Reformed covenant theology. I preserved the substance as God’s eternal saving purpose without expanding it into a detailed covenantal framework.
The language of Christ satisfying justice and magnifying the law assumes a substitutionary atonement framework, which is central to the original and was retained rather than softened.

The original’s severe self-description of human corruption is characteristic of Puritan spirituality. I kept its doctrine of pervasive sin and helplessness while avoiding archaic or needlessly degrading phrasing.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “present and personal interest in Christ” as personally receiving and sharing in Christ’s saving benefits by faith, rather than merely having intellectual belief about him.
I rendered “my religion may not be occasional and partial, but universal, influential, effective” as a request for whole-life faith that shapes every area of life and bears fruit.
I took “continue in thy words as well as thy works” to mean abiding in God’s Word while also walking faithfully in the works and duties God gives, rather than treating “works” as meritorious deeds.
